headword: Allen, Alleine, Alleyne, Allan, Allin, Alland
meaning: the son of Alan, or Allen, or Aleyn (Yonge, i. 396-7)
author_comment: 'Aleyne, propyr name, Alanus': Prompt. Parv. 'Forth goth Alein, the clerk, and also John.'—Chaucer, C. T. 4015. (The d in Alland is an excrescence as in Simmonds.) One of our most popular names while surnames were becoming hereditary; said to have come into England with Alan Fergéant, Count of Brittany, a companion of the Conqueror, and first Earl of Richmond, co. York. Very soon common to north England and the Scottish border. The founder of Dulwich Coll., 1619, was Edward Allen, or Alleyne. Derivatives, Allcock, Allkins, Allnutt, and perhaps Allatt, q.v. Possibly an abbrev. of Alinot; v. Allnutt.
source: Hundred Rolls, 1273
record_text: Henry Aleyn, 1273. A.

meaning: (1) of the Alley, i.e. from residence in a narrow passage; M.E. aley and alley; (2) probably in some cases Alley, a pet-name for Allen and Alice
author_comment: The first instance I possess is that of a foundling, found in an alley. But the name was an older one, of similar but more legitimate descent. The Hundred Rolls instances from Oxford and Cambridge seem very natural, just where we should expect alleys to be found; v. Twitchen. (2) A pet-name for very great favourites, Allen and Alice, q.v.; cf. Charlie, Teddy, &c.
source: Testa de Nevill, sive Liber Feodorum, temp. Hen. III-Edw. I

author_comment: Allgood, like Thoroughgood and Toogood, seems very complimentary, but it is without doubt a baptismal name, as are they. I see Lower says Algod occurs as a personal name before Domesday (Patr. Brit. p. 6).

Alabone, in the Weekly Pulpit for May 22, 1887. Allaband and Alleborn are American variants.
